questions.prompt: Walk through ww7's transitionWorkflowStatus for a request that names a target status: which checks run, in what order, and why is that order the right one?

keyPoints.text: The workflow is loaded unscoped and a missing id answers 404 WORKFLOW_NOT_FOUND before anything else is decided.
Ownership comes next: an ADMIN passes, any other actor must be the workflow's creator or gets 403 WORKFLOW_SCOPE_VIOLATION.
Legality is a single lookup in the allowedTransitions table, made after ownership and before the stored definition is rebuilt or anything is written; ARCHIVED lists no exits, so archiving is final.
The machine deliberately lets an equal pair through, which hands the policy decision for repeats to the service.
keyPoints.quote: The workflow status machine treats current equal next status as valid, so the service must decide whether repetition is a no-op or a fresh audit event.

keyPoints.text: The service's equality return sits after both checks, so the no-op branch is not a way around ownership.
keyPoints.quote: Equality is checked after authorization and state lookup, so an unauthorized actor does not receive a free read path through the no-op branch.

keyPoints.text: Only a genuine move into ACTIVE runs the readiness rules (at least one step, an event name for EVENT, a cron for SCHEDULE, each a 422) and computes the next scheduled time.
The write comes last: updateStatus, then an audit event recording previousStatus and nextStatus.

questions.prompt: Explain how a workflow's status decides whether ww7 ever runs it on its own, and what the status-change audit trail is meant to say. Use pausing and re-activating a scheduled workflow as your example.

keyPoints.text: The scheduler's due query only returns workflows that are ACTIVE, of trigger type SCHEDULE, with nextScheduledAt at or before now.
Event-triggered dispatch filters on ACTIVE in the same way, so a paused or draft workflow is invisible to both automatic paths.
A move to anything but ACTIVE writes nextScheduledAt as null, so pausing clears the schedule; the runtime test asserts the PAUSED update carries null.
Moving back to ACTIVE recomputes the next time from the cron expression rather than restoring the old one.
An audit entry of this kind is a claim that something actually moved.
keyPoints.quote: For operational workflows, a `status.changed` event should describe an actual state change.

keyPoints.text: Only user moves leave a status trail: event dispatch writes a workflow.event.dispatched row per matched workflow, while the scheduler's own advance re-writes the status as ACTIVE and records nothing about it.

The cron text is only parsed when the workflow becomes ACTIVE (the schema checks just its length), so a paused workflow edited to a bad cron is refused at re-activation with 422 INVALID_CRON_EXPRESSION from the schedule helper and stays PAUSED.

questions.prompt: Defend or indict this claim: "Now that ACTIVE to ACTIVE is idempotent, ww7's workflow status is safe under concurrent callers and every status move is audited."

keyPoints.text: The no-op rule is a decision made in application code from a value read earlier; it holds no lock.
keyPoints.quote: This is an application-level idempotency rule, not a database lock.

keyPoints.text: Two callers that both read the same starting status can each write a different target, because the write is not conditional on what was read.
keyPoints.quote: Two concurrent callers can still race on different transitions because the repository update does not carry an old-status predicate

keyPoints.text: The scheduler's advance step also goes through updateStatus and writes ACTIVE explicitly, so a pause or archive that lands between its due read and that write is silently turned back on, attributed to the last editor, with no audit entry for the reversal.
The status write and the audit insert are two separate calls with no transaction; the test pins an audit failure after a completed update, which leaves a moved workflow with no audit record.

The repair direction is a conditional write that names the expected current status (id plus status in the WHERE) and treats zero affected rows as a conflict, with the audit row in the same transaction.
The evidence shipped with the change cannot settle this: it is call-order proof with test doubles.
keyPoints.quote: The runtime evidence proves call ordering with doubles; a live database test is needed for isolation claims.
